name: Tan-extender moisturizer

lead: A tan-extender is a moisturizer people use to keep a self-tan looking fresh for longer. The payoff is colour that stays even and lasts past the usual few days, and some formulas add a little DHA so colour is topped up as you moisturize.

Self-tan colour sits in the dead outer skin layer and fades over roughly 3 to 10 days as that layer sheds. Extenders are marketed as slowing the fade by hydrating the skin. No trial has measured whether they lengthen tan life; the DHA versions add visible colour directly.

paras: People use it as their regular body lotion after a self-tan, usually daily, in place of an ordinary moisturizer. Many pair it with a fresh self-tan application when the colour starts to fade.
A 2024 case report described protein contact dermatitis to one tan-extender lotion, attributed to pumpkin seed oil. As with any lotion, people with ingredient allergies check the label.

angle.text: Tan-extender lotions are used to keep a self-tan looking fresh past the usual 3 to 10 days by keeping the outer skin hydrated while the tanned layer sheds. Some formulas also add a little DHA, which tops up visible colour; no trial has measured the slower-fade effect.

lead: Tan-extender moisturizers are hydrating lotions marketed to keep a sunless (self) tan looking even and lasting longer, so the bronzed colour people want for their look stays on the skin for more days. Self-tan colour from dihydroxyacetone (DHA) sits in the dead outer layer of skin and is described as fading over roughly 3 to 10 days as that layer is shed.[1] Extender products are positioned as slowing that fade, and some contain small amounts of DHA to top up colour.

DHA is described by Wikipedia as reacting with amino acids in the dead outer layer of skin to produce a brown colour, without needing UV light or involving the skin's own pigment, usually at 3 to 5 percent in self-tanners.[1] Spray tans last roughly 5 to 10 days.[1] Because the colour is tied to the shedding skin layer, a lotion used daily to maintain the tan fits naturally into a self-tanning routine.
No published trial has measured whether tan-extender moisturizers lengthen the life of a self-tan. The one indexed medical report concerns an allergic reaction to an ingredient.[2]

paras: Sunless tans fade as the skin cell layer containing the colour is shed, a process lasting about 3 to 10 days.[1] Hydrating products are marketed on the idea that supple skin sheds more slowly, though no published study tested this for these products. Wikipedia's article on sunless tanning does not describe tan extenders as a category.[1]

Erythrulose works similarly to DHA but develops more slowly, and both can cause contact dermatitis.[1] Bronzers are temporary cosmetic colour that washes off with soap and water and are often used to complement a DHA tan.[1]

Eva Wittgenstein of Cincinnati Children's Hospital found DHA's skin-browning effect in the 1950s, when an oral treatment stained skin. Man-Tan, the first commercial DHA self-tanner, appeared in 1959, followed by Coppertone's Quick Tan in 1960; early products gave orange tones, and automated spray booths broadened the market from the late 1990s.[1]

A 2024 case report in Contact Dermatitis described protein contact dermatitis to a tan-extender lotion, with the authors assessing pumpkin seed oil (Luffa cylindrica seed oil) as the probable cause.[2] It is a single report and does not give a rate of reactions.

For DHA tanning generally, Wikipedia reports that the FDA has approved DHA for external use only, not around eyes, lips, mucous membranes or for inhalation, and that self-tanners themselves provide no UV protection.[1]

timeline.event: Man-Tan, the first commercial DHA self-tanner, appears.[1]
